```{r setup, include=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(modelr)
library(p8105.datasets)

knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  fig.width = 8,
  fig.asp = 0.65,
  out.width = "90%",
  message = FALSE,
  warning = FALSE
)
theme_set(theme_minimal() + theme(legend.position = "bottom"))
set.seed(2026)
```

## Problem 1: Homicide investigations

```{r homicide-clean}
homicide_df =
  read_csv("data/homicide-data.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(
    city_state = str_c(city, state, sep = ", "),
    resolved = as.numeric(disposition == "Closed by arrest"),
    victim_age = as.numeric(victim_age),
    victim_race = factor(victim_race, levels = c("White", "Black")),
    victim_sex = factor(victim_sex, levels = c("Female", "Male"))
  ) |>
  filter(
    !city_state %in% c("Dallas, TX", "Phoenix, AZ", "Kansas City, MO", "Tulsa, AL"),
    victim_race %in% c("White", "Black")
  ) |>
  drop_na(resolved, victim_age, victim_sex, victim_race)

homicide_df |>
  count(city_state, name = "number_of_cases") |>
  knitr::kable()
```

`resolved = 1` denotes cases closed by arrest; `resolved = 0` denotes cases not closed by arrest. 
The comparison of interest is **Male versus Female**, holding victim age and race fixed.

### Baltimore logistic regression

```{r baltimore-model}
baltimore_fit =
  homicide_df |>
  filter(city_state == "Baltimore, MD") |>
  glm(resolved ~ victim_age + victim_sex + victim_race,
      data = _, family = binomial())

broom::tidy(baltimore_fit) |>
  mutate(
    adjusted_or = exp(estimate),
    or_ci_lower = exp(estimate - 1.96 * std.error),
    or_ci_upper = exp(estimate + 1.96 * std.error)
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)

baltimore_result =
  broom::tidy(baltimore_fit) |>
  filter(term == "victim_sexMale") |>
  transmute(
    city_state = "Baltimore, MD",
    adjusted_or = exp(estimate),
    lower_ci = exp(estimate - 1.96 * std.error),
    upper_ci = exp(estimate + 1.96 * std.error)
  )

baltimore_result |> knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

The adjusted odds ratio for case resolution comparing male victims with female victims in Baltimore 
is `r round(baltimore_result$adjusted_or, 3)` (95% CI: `r round(baltimore_result$lower_ci, 3)` to 
`r round(baltimore_result$upper_ci, 3)`). 
An odds ratio less than 1 indicates lower adjusted odds of a case being closed by arrest for male victims; 
an odds ratio greater than 1 indicates higher adjusted odds.

### Fit a model for each city

```{r city-models}
city_or_df =
  homicide_df |>
  nest(city_data = -city_state) |>
  mutate(
    models = map(city_data, \(df) glm(
      resolved ~ victim_age + victim_sex + victim_race,
      data = df, family = binomial()
    )),
    estimates = map(models, broom::tidy)
  ) |>
  select(city_state, estimates) |>
  unnest(estimates) |>
  filter(term == "victim_sexMale") |>
  transmute(
    city_state,
    adjusted_or = exp(estimate),
    lower_ci = exp(estimate - 1.96 * std.error),
    upper_ci = exp(estimate + 1.96 * std.error)
  ) |>
  arrange(adjusted_or)

city_or_df |> knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

### Plot the adjusted odds ratios

```{r city-plot, fig.height=10}
city_or_df |>
  mutate(city_state = fct_reorder(city_state, adjusted_or)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = adjusted_or, y = city_state)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray40") +
  geom_errorbar(aes(xmin = lower_ci, xmax = upper_ci), width = 0.2) +
  geom_point(size = 1.7, color = "steelblue4") +
  labs(
    title = "Adjusted odds of homicide resolution: male versus female victims",
    subtitle = "Odds ratios adjusted for victim age and race; 95% Wald confidence intervals",
    x = "Adjusted odds ratio (male vs. female)",
    y = "City"
  )
```

The graph orders cities by their adjusted odds ratios. The dashed vertical line indicates an odds ratio of 1.
Estimates to the left of 1 indicate lower odds of resolution for male victims, while estimates to the right indicate higher odds. 
Confidence intervals crossing 1 do not provide strong evidence of a sex difference at the 5% significance level.

## Problem 2: Bootstrap inference

```{r weather-clean}
data("weather_df")
weather_analysis =
  weather_df |>
  select(tmax, tmin, prcp) |>
  drop_na()

weather_fit = lm(tmax ~ tmin + prcp, data = weather_analysis)

broom::tidy(weather_fit) |> knitr::kable(digits = 3)
broom::glance(weather_fit) |>
  select(r.squared, adj.r.squared, sigma) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

The estimated coefficient ratio below is `beta_tmin / beta_prcp`, where both slopes are taken 
from the regression `tmax ~ tmin + prcp`. Their units differ, so the ratio is a mathematical 
summary rather than a dimensionless effect measure.

```{r bootstrap-models}
set.seed(2026)
boot_results =
  weather_analysis |>
  modelr::bootstrap(n = 5000) |>
  mutate(
    models = map(strap, \(df) lm(tmax ~ tmin + prcp, data = df)),
    r_squared = map_dbl(models, \(fit) broom::glance(fit)$r.squared),
    beta_ratio = map_dbl(models, \(fit) {
      betas = coef(fit)
      unname(betas["tmin"] / betas["prcp"])
    })
  ) |>
  select(r_squared, beta_ratio)

boot_results |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "quantity", values_to = "estimate") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = estimate)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40, fill = "steelblue", color = "white") +
  facet_wrap(~ quantity, scales = "free", ncol = 1) +
  labs(
    title = "Bootstrap distributions from 5,000 resamples",
    x = "Bootstrap estimate", y = "Count"
  )
```

```{r bootstrap-intervals}
boot_summary =
  boot_results |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "quantity", values_to = "estimate") |>
  group_by(quantity) |>
  summarize(
    bootstrap_mean = mean(estimate),
    lower_ci = quantile(estimate, 0.025),
    upper_ci = quantile(estimate, 0.975),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

boot_summary |> knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

Based on 5,000 bootstrap samples, the percentile 95% confidence interval for the regression R-squared 
is [`r round(boot_summary$lower_ci[boot_summary$quantity == "r_squared"], 3)`, 
`r round(boot_summary$upper_ci[boot_summary$quantity == "r_squared"], 3)`]. 
The percentile 95% confidence interval for the ratio of the `tmin` and `prcp` coefficients 
is [`r round(boot_summary$lower_ci[boot_summary$quantity == "beta_ratio"], 3)`, 
`r round(boot_summary$upper_ci[boot_summary$quantity == "beta_ratio"], 3)`]. 
The plots display the sampling variability approximated by bootstrap resampling. 
The ratio may be skewed or unstable if the estimated precipitation coefficient is near zero.

## Problem 3: Modeling birthweight

```{r birthweight-clean}
birthweight_df =
  read_csv("data/birthweight.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(
    babysex = factor(babysex, levels = c(1, 2), labels = c("male", "female")),
    malform = factor(malform, levels = c(0, 1), labels = c("absent", "present")),
    frace = factor(frace),
    mrace = factor(mrace)
  )

birthweight_df |> summarize(
  n = n(),
  missing_values = sum(is.na(birthweight_df)),
  mean_birthweight_g = mean(bwt),
  sd_birthweight_g = sd(bwt)
) |> knitr::kable(digits = 2)
```

### Proposed model

I selected predictors based on their plausible associations with birthweight: infant head circumference and birth length describe newborn size; gestational age reflects duration of fetal growth; maternal smoking and weight gain describe pregnancy exposures; and pre-pregnancy BMI, maternal age, and infant sex are additional maternal and infant characteristics.

```{r proposed-model}
my_model = lm(
  bwt ~ bhead + blength + gaweeks + smoken + wtgain + ppbmi + momage + babysex,
  data = birthweight_df
)

broom::tidy(my_model) |> knitr::kable(digits = 3)
broom::glance(my_model) |>
  select(r.squared, adj.r.squared, sigma) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

### Residuals versus fitted values

```{r residual-plot}
birthweight_df |>
  modelr::add_predictions(my_model) |>
  modelr::add_residuals(my_model) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = pred, y = resid)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.25, color = "steelblue") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE, color = "firebrick") +
  labs(
    title = "Residuals versus fitted values for the proposed model",
    x = "Fitted birthweight (g)", y = "Residual (g)"
  )
```

The residuals are generally centered around zero, particularly for fitted birthweights 
between 2,500 and 4,000 grams. However, the LOESS smooth curve shows some curvature, 
especially at lower fitted values, suggesting that the model may not fully capture nonlinear relationships. 
Several large residuals are also present, indicating potential outliers. 
Overall, the model appears reasonable, although some model misspecification may remain.

### Compare prediction error

```{r cv-models}
set.seed(2026)
cv_df =
  modelr::crossv_mc(birthweight_df, 100) |>
  mutate(
    train = map(train, as_tibble),
    test = map(test, as_tibble),
    proposed_fit = map(train, \(df) lm(
      bwt ~ bhead + blength + gaweeks + smoken + wtgain + ppbmi + momage + babysex,
      data = df
    )),
    length_ga_fit = map(train, \(df) lm(bwt ~ blength + gaweeks, data = df)),
    interaction_fit = map(train, \(df) lm(
      bwt ~ (bhead + blength + babysex)^3, data = df
    )),
    rmse_proposed = map2_dbl(proposed_fit, test, modelr::rmse),
    rmse_length_ga = map2_dbl(length_ga_fit, test, modelr::rmse),
    rmse_interaction = map2_dbl(interaction_fit, test, modelr::rmse)
  )

cv_results =
  cv_df |>
  select(starts_with("rmse_")) |>
  pivot_longer(
    everything(),
    names_to = "model",
    names_prefix = "rmse_",
    values_to = "rmse"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    model = recode(model,
      "proposed" = "Proposed model",
      "length_ga" = "Length + gestational age",
      "interaction" = "Three-way interaction model"
    )
  )

cv_results |>
  group_by(model) |>
  summarize(
    mean_rmse = mean(rmse),
    sd_rmse = sd(rmse),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  arrange(mean_rmse) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 2)
```

```{r cv-plot}
cv_results |>
  ggplot(aes(x = model, y = rmse, fill = model)) +
  geom_violin(alpha = 0.7, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.15, alpha = 0.7, show.legend = FALSE) +
  labs(
    title = "Cross-validated prediction error across 100 random splits",
    x = NULL, y = "Test-set RMSE (g)"
  ) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 15, hjust = 1))
```

```{r best-model, include=FALSE}
cv_summary = cv_results |>
  group_by(model) |>
  summarize(mean_rmse = mean(rmse), .groups = "drop") |>
  arrange(mean_rmse)
```

Based on 100 Monte Carlo cross-validation splits, the proposed model had the lowest mean test-set RMSE, 
followed by the three-way interaction model and the length plus gestational age model. 
The proposed model also had the smallest standard deviation of RMSE, 
indicating relatively consistent predictive performance across the random splits.

Although the three-way interaction model includes more complex relationships among predictors, 
it did not improve out-of-sample prediction accuracy compared with the proposed model. 
The model using only birth length and gestational age performed substantially worse, 
suggesting that additional predictors provide useful information for predicting birthweight.

Overall, the proposed model is preferred among the three models evaluated, as it achieved 
the lowest cross-validated prediction error and the most consistent performance across splits. 
However, the residual plot suggests that some nonlinear patterns or outliers may not be fully accounted for.
